title: Texts in Art, Ritual and American Life
bigQuestion: How do Buddhist texts live beyond the page, in art, ritual and American life, and what does respectful engagement with them look like?

story.title: A Week of Sand
story.kicker: Monks spend days building a mandala of colored sand in a museum, and then sweep it away.
paragraphs: On a Monday morning, a small group of Tibetan monks arrives at a museum. They chant, then draw careful lines on a low, flat platform. Over the next days they lay down colored sand, grain by grain, from narrow metal funnels called chakpur. They rub a rod along the ridged funnel, and the vibration lets a thin stream of sand fall.

Visitors crowd around. The design grows from the center outward: a palace seen from above, with gates on four sides, rings of symbols and bands of color. Tibetan tradition calls it a *mandala*, a sacred diagram. Each detail follows texts and teachers passed down for centuries. Some visitors come back every day to watch.

On the last day, the monks chant again. Then one of them draws lines through the design, from the edges to the center, and the sand is swept into a pile. Some of it is given to visitors in small packets. The rest is carried in an urn to a nearby river and poured into the water, which the monks describe as sending its blessing into the world.

Groups of monks, such as those from Drepung Loseling Monastery, have made sand mandalas like this in American museums and universities since the late 1980s. For the monks, it is a religious practice. For many visitors, it is also a lesson about impermanence. This chapter looks at how Buddhist texts and teachings live in art, ritual and American life.
story.think: Why might a tradition choose to destroy a beautiful thing it worked so hard to make?

lessons.title: Copying the Heart Sutra
lessons.mainIdea: In East Asia, copying sutras by hand, especially the short Heart Sutra, is a devotional practice that Buddhists believe brings merit.
reading: The *Heart Sutra* is one of the shortest and best-known Mahayana texts. In the common Chinese version, credited to the monk Xuanzang in the seventh century, it has about 260 characters. It teaches, through the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. It ends with a mantra. Monks and laypeople across East Asia recite it daily.

Copying sutras is an old devotional act. Some Mahayana sutras, such as the Lotus Sutra, praise the merit of copying them. In Japan, *shakyo*, sutra copying, is practiced at temples and at home. A person grinds ink, sits quietly and copies the Heart Sutra character by character with a brush, often over a faint model. Many temples accept the finished copies as offerings.

This practice treats the text as more than information. The act of copying is itself valued, and the finished page is treated with care. In the eighth century, Japanese court workshops copied thousands of sutra scrolls. Today calligraphers also make Heart Sutra art. Buddhists often ask that such art be displayed respectfully, not on floors or in bathrooms.

words.d: a very short Mahayana sutra on emptiness, recited daily across East Asia
the Japanese practice of copying sutras by hand as devotion
good karma Buddhists believe comes from good actions such as copying sutras
a sacred phrase or syllable recited in Buddhist and Hindu practice

look.title: Form and Emptiness
look.text: Avalokiteshvara, practicing deep wisdom, sees that the five aggregates are empty. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form.
look.cite: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita Hrdaya), Chinese text attributed to Xuanzang (649 CE); paraphrased (cf. tr. Red Pine, The Heart Sutra, 2004)
look.prompt: Which classical reader from Unit 15 would find this line most familiar, and why?

check.q: About how many characters are in the common Chinese Heart Sutra?
check.why: The Heart Sutra is famously short, about 260 characters.

check.q: What is shakyo?
choices: Copying sutras by hand as devotion
check.why: Shakyo is Japanese sutra copying.

check.q: What does the Heart Sutra teach about form?
choices: Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form
check.why: This is its best-known line.

lessons.title: Texts at Death
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhist communities recite texts at funerals and memorials, and each tradition chooses different texts for the dying and the dead.
reading: Some of the most important uses of Buddhist texts come at death. In Theravada countries, monks chant passages from the Abhidhamma and suttas at funerals and memorial rites. A common verse says that conditioned things are impermanent and that their calming is happiness. Families offer food and robes to monks and share the merit with the dead.

In Japanese Jodo Shinshu and other Pure Land temples, ministers chant from the Pure Land sutras and recite *nembutsu*, Namu Amida Butsu, the name of Amida Buddha. Families gather at memorial services held on set anniversaries after a death. The Buddhist Temple of Chicago, a Jodo Shinshu-rooted community, holds such services for its members.

In Tibetan traditions, a lama may read the text known in English as the Tibetan Book of the Dead, the Bardo Thodol, to guide a dying or dead person through the *bardo*, the in-between state. It was first translated into English by Kazi Dawa Samdup and edited by W.Y. Evans-Wentz in 1927. Each tradition chooses texts that match its teaching about death.

words.d: reciting 'Namu Amida Butsu,' the name of Amida Buddha, in Pure Land Buddhism
in Tibetan Buddhism, the in-between state after death and before rebirth
a gathering to honor someone who has died, often on set anniversaries

look.title: Three Funerals
look.text: Bangkok: monks chant in Pali; the family pours water to share merit. Chicago: a minister leads 'Namu Amida Butsu' at a memorial service. Dharamsala: a lama reads the Bardo Thodol beside the body.
look.prompt: What does each choice of text suggest about that tradition's view of what happens at death?

check.q: What is the nembutsu?
check.why: The nembutsu is central in Pure Land practice.

check.q: What is the bardo?
check.why: Tibetan texts describe the bardo between death and rebirth.

check.q: Who edited the 1927 English Tibetan Book of the Dead?
check.why: Evans-Wentz edited Kazi Dawa Samdup's translation.

lessons.title: The Lotus and a Chant
lessons.mainIdea: Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra, treating the name of a text as the heart of their practice.
reading: The *Lotus Sutra* is a Mahayana sutra that teaches, among other things, that all beings can become Buddhas and that the Buddha's life is vast beyond measure. It was translated into Chinese by Kumarajiva in 406 CE. East Asian Buddhists have honored it for centuries, and Tiantai thinkers placed it at the summit of the sutras.

In thirteenth-century Japan, the monk Nichiren (1222 to 1282) taught that chanting the sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, contains the whole of its power. Nichiren Buddhists today, including members of Soka Gakkai International and Nichiren Shu temples, chant the title, the *daimoku*, often before a scroll called the Gohonzon.

Here the text lives most fully in a phrase. Nichiren Buddhists believe chanting it expresses and awakens Buddha-nature. Soka Gakkai has members in many countries, including the United States. Scholars note how this practice differs from Theravada study of the suttas, and see both as ways of treating a text as a living presence.

words.d: a Mahayana sutra teaching that all beings can become Buddhas
the chanted title of the Lotus Sutra, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo
a Japanese Buddhist teacher (1222-1282) who taught chanting the Lotus Sutra's title

look.title: The Lotus Sutra Through Time
look.cite: Burton Watson, The Lotus Sutra (1993); standard histories of Tiantai and Nichiren Buddhism
look.prompt: About how many centuries passed between the Chinese translation and Nichiren?

check.q: Who translated the Lotus Sutra into Chinese in 406 CE?
check.why: Kumarajiva's translation became standard in East Asia.

check.q: What do Nichiren Buddhists chant?
check.why: The daimoku is the Lotus Sutra's title.

check.q: What does the Lotus Sutra teach, among other things?
choices: The Vinaya is the only text
check.why: Its teaching of universal Buddhahood is central.

lessons.title: Made to Be Swept Away
lessons.mainIdea: Tibetan sand mandalas are built as sacred diagrams following ritual texts and then dissolved, a practice monks link to impermanence and blessing.
reading: A *mandala* in Tibetan Buddhism is a diagram of a sacred world: the palace of a Buddha or deity, seen from above. Its forms follow tantric texts and ritual manuals, and monks spend years learning to draw them. Sand mandalas are one kind; others are painted on cloth, called thangkas, or built in three dimensions.

One often-made sand mandala is that of Kalachakra, the Wheel of Time. The Dalai Lama has given the Kalachakra initiation many times, including in the United States. Making the mandala is itself a ritual, begun and ended with chanting. The monks describe it as consecrating the space and blessing those who see it.

The dissolution is part of the practice. Monks explain it as a teaching on *impermanence* and as a way of spreading blessing, especially when the sand goes into flowing water. Museum visitors often see it as art. Monks usually welcome visitors while asking for quiet respect. Scholars note that the museum setting adds new meanings while the ritual keeps its own.

words.d: a sacred diagram of a Buddha's or deity's world, often seen from above
the Wheel of Time: a Tibetan tantric system and its mandala
anicca: the teaching that all conditioned things change and end
a Tibetan Buddhist painting on cloth, often of a deity or mandala

look.title: Two Viewers
look.text: A monk: we build the mandala as an offering and consecrate the space; we dissolve it to show impermanence and to bless the waters. A museum visitor: it is the most beautiful artwork I have seen, and I can't believe they destroyed it.
look.prompt: How can both viewers be describing something real? What does each miss?

check.q: What does a Tibetan mandala show?
choices: A sacred world or palace seen from above
check.why: Mandalas depict a Buddha's or deity's realm.

check.q: What is Kalachakra?
choices: The Wheel of Time, a tantric system and mandala
check.why: Kalachakra means Wheel of Time.

check.q: How do monks explain the dissolution of the mandala?
choices: As a teaching on impermanence and a way to spread blessing
check.why: Monks link it to impermanence and blessing.

lessons.title: Stupas and the First Images
lessons.mainIdea: Early Buddhist art honored the Buddha with symbols and stupas; images of the Buddha in human form appear around the first century CE.
reading: The earliest Buddhist monuments are *stupas*, mounds over relics, as the Mahaparinibbana Sutta describes. At Sanchi and Bharhut, carvings from the last centuries BCE show scenes of the Buddha's life. But in many of them, the Buddha himself is not shown as a person. Instead there is an empty seat, a tree, footprints, a wheel or a parasol.

Scholars long called this aniconic art, art without images, and debated why. Some thought early Buddhists avoided showing the Buddha. Others, such as Susan Huntington, argued that some scenes show later worship at sacred sites rather than the Buddha himself. The debate continues. It is a good case of scholars reading the same evidence in different ways.

Around the first century CE, images of the Buddha in human form appear in two regions: Gandhara, in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan, with Greek-influenced styles, and Mathura, in northern India. From then on, the *Buddha image* spread across Asia in countless styles. Buddhists treat these images with deep respect, as reminders of the Buddha and, for many, as objects of devotion that are consecrated in ritual.

words.d: a dome-shaped monument over relics, honored by walking around it
without images; art that uses symbols instead of showing a figure
a statue or painting of the Buddha, honored by Buddhists and often consecrated
an ancient region in today's Pakistan and Afghanistan known for early Buddha images

look.title: Early Buddhist Art Sites
look.cite: Susan L. Huntington, The Art of Ancient India (1985); UNESCO listings for Sanchi and Borobudur
look.prompt: Put these in order. What changes in how the Buddha is shown?

check.q: What symbols stand for the Buddha in some early carvings?
choices: An empty seat, a tree, footprints or a wheel
check.why: Early art often shows symbols instead of a figure.

check.q: Where did early Buddha images in human form appear?
check.why: Both regions produced early images around the first century CE.

check.q: What did Susan Huntington argue about some 'aniconic' scenes?
choices: They may show later worship at sacred sites
check.why: Her reading challenged the older view.

lessons.title: The Buddha as Decor
lessons.mainIdea: Many Buddhists object to Buddha images used as casual decor, tattoos or products, and communities differ on where the lines fall.
reading: Buddha statues are sold in garden centers, used as bar decor and printed on swimwear. For many Buddhists, this is painful. A *consecrated* image in a temple is treated as a presence: people bow, offer flowers and light, and place it high. Seeing the same form on a floor, near shoes or in a bathroom can feel like disrespect toward a teacher.

Some countries have acted. Sri Lanka has rules on the display and sale of Buddha images and has turned away tourists with visible Buddha tattoos. Thailand has campaigned against using Buddha heads as decoration and restricts the export of Buddha images. Buddhist groups in Asia and the United States have protested products that use the Buddha as a joke or mascot.

Views vary. Some Buddhist teachers say the image is a reminder, and its presence anywhere can plant a good seed. Others ask that it always be placed high, kept clean and never used for profit or jokes. A respectful rule of thumb from many temples: treat an image as you would treat a picture of a revered teacher. This course follows that *norm*.

words.d: made sacred through a ritual; many Buddha images in temples are consecrated
a shared expectation about how to act
objects used only to decorate a space

look.title: Where Does It Belong?
look.text: Case 1: a Buddha statue on a shelf above eye level in a family room, with fresh flowers. Case 2: a Buddha head as a doorstop. Case 3: a museum display with a label explaining the image's history and use. Case 4: a cartoon Buddha on a beer label.
look.prompt: How might a temple community respond to each case? Explain their reasons, not your own verdict.

check.q: Why do many Buddhists object to Buddha images as casual decor?
choices: They treat images with the respect due to a revered teacher
check.why: Consecrated images are treated as a presence and honored.

check.q: Which country has turned away tourists with visible Buddha tattoos?
check.why: Sri Lanka has enforced rules on Buddha imagery.

check.q: What rule of thumb do many temples give?
choices: Treat an image as you would a picture of a revered teacher
check.why: Placing images high and clean shows respect.

lessons.title: Mindfulness in Schools and Hospitals
lessons.mainIdea: Mindfulness programs drawn from Buddhist teachings are now used in hospitals and schools, and Buddhists and scholars debate what is gained and lost.
reading: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn founded the Stress Reduction Clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. His Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, *MBSR*, drew on Buddhist teachings about sati, mindfulness, and on meditation he had learned from Zen and Theravada teachers. He presented it in secular terms for patients with pain and stress.

MBSR and programs based on it spread widely. Hospitals, the military, businesses and many schools now offer them. Researchers have studied their effects, with results that are promising in some areas and mixed or uncertain in others. Public schools that use such programs usually present them as secular skills for attention and calm, not as religious practice.

Buddhist and scholarly responses vary. Some Buddhist teachers welcome mindfulness as a gift that reduces suffering. Others, and critics such as Ronald Purser in McMindfulness (2019), argue that removing ethics and the path turns a religious practice into a tool for productivity. Some Asian American Buddhists note that the Asian teachers behind the practice are often left out. Describing these views is itself a matter of *attribution*.

words.d: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, a secular program founded by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979
mindfulness: steady awareness, as the suttas describe it
not religious; presented without religious claims
naming whose view or idea something is

look.title: Three Views of Mindfulness
look.text: A hospital nurse: MBSR helped my patients manage pain. A Theravada monk: mindfulness in the suttas is part of an eightfold path that includes ethics. A critic: stripped of ethics, it can help people adjust to harmful conditions instead of changing them.
look.prompt: What does each speaker focus on? Report the three views in one fair paragraph.

check.q: Who founded MBSR in 1979?
check.why: Kabat-Zinn founded it at the University of Massachusetts.

check.q: How do public school mindfulness programs usually present themselves?
choices: As secular skills for attention and calm
check.why: Schools present them in secular terms.

check.q: What does the 'McMindfulness' critique argue?
choices: Removing ethics turns practice into a productivity tool
check.why: Purser's critique centers on the loss of ethics and context.

lessons.title: Temples as Communities
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Buddhist temples, from the Buddhist Temple of Chicago founded in 1944 to many newer communities, are places where texts are lived week by week.
reading: Chicago's Buddhist history has two famous early dates. In 1893, Anagarika Dharmapala of Sri Lanka and the Japanese Zen teacher Soyen Shaku spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions, held with the World's Columbian Exposition. Many historians see it as a key moment for Buddhism in America. In 1944, Rev. Gyomay Kubose founded the Buddhist Temple of Chicago.

Kubose's temple grew among Japanese Americans who came to Chicago after the wartime incarceration camps. It offered services, Dharma school for children and a community in a new city. Since then, Chicago and its suburbs have become home to temples and centers of many traditions, founded by Thai, Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, Chinese, Korean, Sri Lankan, Tibetan and other communities, and by convert groups.

In these *sanghas*, the texts are lived. Children learn verses. Families chant for the dead. Monks give talks on a sutta. Volunteers cook for festivals. For many immigrant families, the temple also keeps language and culture alive. A student who visits, with permission and respect, sees that Buddhist texts are not only studied in classrooms. They are part of Illinois life.

words.d: a Buddhist community; also the community of monks and nuns
a Sunday or weekend school where Buddhist children learn teachings and practices
imprisonment; Japanese Americans were forced into camps during World War II

lessons.title: Visiting With Respect
lessons.mainIdea: A respectful visit to a temple follows its customs, asks permission, and treats practitioners as teachers of their own tradition.
reading: Many Chicago-area temples welcome visitors, especially school groups who call ahead. Customs vary, but some are common. Visitors often remove shoes before entering the shrine hall. They dress modestly, speak quietly, and do not point their feet toward the Buddha image or a monk. They ask before taking photos. They do not touch images or ritual objects.

Visitors are not expected to bow or chant. In this course, you *observe*; you do not practice. If a ceremony is taking place, you watch quietly. If a monk or member offers to explain, you listen and ask thoughtful questions. Many temples are glad to share, and practitioners are the best teachers of what their own practices mean.

After a visit, a good report describes what was seen and heard, names who explained it, and uses the community's own words. It does not judge. It does not treat the temple as exotic or strange. It treats neighbors as neighbors. This is the same *respect* the course has asked for throughout: describe, attribute, and honor what others hold sacred.

words.d: to watch and note carefully without taking part
treating people and what they hold sacred with care and courtesy
the main room in a temple, where the Buddha image is placed

check.q: What is the student's role at a temple visit in this course?
check.why: The course describes practice and never leads it.

check.why: Describe, attribute and respect.
